questions.text: A team added the DAX in front of the DynamoDB to speed up readings, but realized that part of the calls continues to go straight to the bank without cash gain. Analysis showed that these calls use ConsistentRead=true. What is the explanation?
options: The DAX only cache tables with less than 1 GB
The DAX needs to be restarted daily to cache everything
The DAX attends the cache only possibly consistent readings; strongly consistent readings are passed directly to DynamoDB
The cluster DAX is on another account
questions.explanation: By design, or DAX does not serve strongly consistent cache read(s) — applications that require strong consistency do not benefit from DAX in these calls.
questions.hint: The accelerator serves the 'freeze' reading of the cache; whoever requires the certified data at the time drills the cache row.
optionRationales: By design, or DAX does not serve strongly consistent cache read(s) — applications that require strong consistency do not benefit from DAX in these calls.
There is no daily restart — the observed behavior is the documented semantic consistency.
Account configuration would generate connection/permission errors — no selective bypass by type of reading.
There is no such limit — the bypass criterion is the mode of consistency of reading.

questions.text: Consumers in a row SQS they are not following the production of messages, and the processing delay grows. SQS is the best indicator of this backlog and how it can guide automatic correction?
options: The average body size of the messages
NumberOfMessagesDeleted, showing future delay
The color of the row icon on the console
ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible: row size can feed an alarm/target tracking that scales consumers (ex: ASG or competition) as backlog grows
questions.explanation: The depth of the row is the production×consumption imbalance thermometer — using it (or the backlog by instance) as a consumer scaling metric closes the automatic correction cycle.
questions.hint: Tell me how many messages are 'in the waiting room' — and use that number to hire more attendants alone.
optionRationales: The depth of the row is the production×consumption imbalance thermometer — using it (or the backlog by instance) as a consumer scaling metric closes the automatic correction cycle.
Exclusions measure what has already been processed — accumulated backlog appears in visible messages waiting.
The non-color backlog console — serious monitoring uses metrics and alarms.
Average Payload reports unit weight — not accumulation of unprocessed messages.

questions.text: A function Lambda consumes a stream of Kinesis and the dashboard shows the IteratorAge metric growing continuously. What this means and what are the typical correction levers?
options: The stream's been empty for a long time.
The function is with excessive permissions
Processing is delayed in relation to the arrival of records (risk of expiring retention data); correct by accelerating the function, increasing parallelism factor/shards or batch size
Records are coming from the future with wrong timestamps
questions.explanation: IteratorAge measures the age of the last processed record: constant growth indicates slower consumption than production — corrections attack consumer throughput before records expire from the retention window.
questions.hint: It is the 'reader's delay' in relation to the treadmill: if it only grows, the reading needs more speed or more readers.
optionRationales: IteratorAge measures the age of the last processed record: constant growth indicates slower consumption than production — corrections attack consumer throughput before records expire from the retention window.
The metric measures the delay of CONSUMO — not the quality of producers' timestamps.
Ozy stream zero or delay — IteratorAge High requires traffic ENTRANDO Faster than it comes out..
Broad permissions are a matter of safety — they do not affect the stream's consumption speed.

questions.text: A route from API Gateway calls for processing that takes ~50 seconds, and TODAS calls return error 504 What limit explains the error and what architectural pattern the contour?
options: Error CORS in long calls
Lack of memory in API Gateway, which should be resized
The certificate TLS expired

The integration timeout of the API Gateway (~29 seconds in the pattern) is exceeded; the correction is the asynchronous pattern: the API thread/start work and return 202 with an ID for the customer consult the status
questions.explanation: The gateway does not indefinitely wait for the backend: long works must be uncoupled (SQS/Step Functions) with immediate response and polling/webhook completion — eliminating the 504 structural.
questions.hint: The gateway shuts down the call near the 29s — delayed work receives a 'service protocol' and rotates behind the scenes.
optionRationales: The gateway does not indefinitely wait for the backend: long works must be uncoupled (SQS/Step Functions) with immediate response and polling/webhook completion — eliminating the 504 structural.
The gateway is managed without memory dimensioning by the customer — the error arises from time, not from resources.
CORS lock in the browser with own errors — or 504 indicates timeout upstream.
Passed certificate fails the handshake immediately — not after 29 seconds of waiting.

questions.text: The latency alarm of a API uses the Media response time and never shoots, but users complain of severe sporadic slowness. What change in monitoring captures this real experience best?
options: Remove the alarm, since the average is healthy
Alarm about high percentages (p95/p99) of latency, which expose the slow tail diluted by the mean
Increase the alarm period to 24 hours
Change the mean to the minimum latency
questions.explanation: The average hides extremes: with 1% of the calls carrying 10s, p99 screams while the average sleeps — high percentages reflect the experience of the most affected users and are the standard for SLOs.
questions.hint: The average hides the 1% Unlucky; the 'p-ninety-and-so' put them in the spotlight.
optionRationales: The average hides extremes: with 1% of the calls carrying 10s, p99 screams while the average sleeps — high percentages reflect the experience of the most affected users and are the standard for SLOs.
The minimum shows the MELHOR called — even blinder to slow tail than average.
Long periods dilute peaks even more — the problem is statistics, not the window.
The users' complaint is the real signal — the monitoring is that you need to see it.

questions.text: In peak traffic, functions Lambda which access a RDS PostgreSQL start failing with 'FATAL: too many connections'. Each concurrent execution opens its own connection. Which service structurally resolves this exhaustion?
options: Create a read replica to receive excess writings
Reduce the timeout of functions to release connections
Amazon RDS Proxy between functions and the bank, multiplexing thousands of executions in a controlled connection pool
Increase max_connections indefinitely not parameter group
questions.explanation: The RDS Proxy shares and reuses connections, absorbing the explosive nature of the serverless without bursting the max_connections — in addition to speeding failovers and integrating with Secrets Manager.
questions.hint: Between the functions swarm and the bank, there is a lack of the 'connection porter' that recycles instead of opening new ones.
optionRationales: The RDS Proxy shares and reuses connections, absorbing the explosive nature of the serverless without bursting the max_connections — in addition to speeding failovers and integrating with Secrets Manager.
Each connection consumes the bank's memory — raising the roof without control only moves the collapse point.
Replicas do not accept written — do not absorb the transactional volume of functions.
Timeout minor kills legitimate executions — the problem is the absence of pooling, not the duration.

questions.text: Seeking to reduce computer costs of Lambda without losing performance, a team evaluates migrating compatible functions to the arm64 architecture (Graviton). What is the expected gain and what care is needed?

Cost per millisecond around 20% lower performance equal or better; it is necessary to validate that dependencies with native binary are compatible with ARM
Migration requires rewriting the code in Rust
Arm64 is free of charge for functions up to 1 GB

There is no gratuitousness by architecture — the gain is the price per GB-second reduced.
Supported runtimes continue to be the same — architecture changes by configuration, not language.
Logging works identically in both architectures.

questions.text: A high volume application needs to publish custom business metrics on each request, but the PutMetricData synchronous calls add latency and cost of API. What is the alternative? CloudWatch offers to emit metrics in scale without extra calls?
options: Record the metrics in a spreadsheet at S3
Call PutMetricData twice to ensure
Customized metrics do not work in high volume
Embedded Metric Format (EMF): Save structured logs to format EMF and the CloudWatch automatically extract the metrics asynchronously

optionRationales: With EMF, the metric travels within the already issued log (stdout)/CloudWatch Logs): no additional synchronous calls, with high cardinality available and raw events preserved for analysis.
Duplicate cost and latency double calls — the opposite of the sought optimization.
Bucket files didn't see alarm metrics from CloudWatch — outside the monitoring ecosystem.
They function — or EMF there is exactly for the high volume and low overhead path.

questions.text: Tasks of a service ECS are being closed repeatedly right after the climb, and the service never stabilizes. What are the first places to investigate the cause of interruptions?
options: The bill of the account, because tasks stop for lack of payment
Delete cluster and recreate from zero immediately
The 'stopped reason' of the closed tasks (console/describe-tasks), the container logs in CloudWatch and service event history (health check failure, memory failure, image pull error))
The number of tags in the task definition

optionRationales: The ECS records the reason for stopping each task (OutOfMemory, failure of ELB health check, CannotPullContainer) and service events narrate the cycle — combined with container logs, close the diagnosis.
Recreate without diagnosis repeats the problem — the cause is recorded in the reasons for stopping and logs.
Suspension for collection would affect the entire account with warnings — not individual loop tasks.
Tags are metadata — don't influence task life cycle.

questions.text: A function Lambda critical need for visibility beyond standard metrics: real memory usage, CPU, network and cold start by running, with dashboards ready. Which feature provides this deep telemetry of functions?
options: The standard metrics already show memory usage per execution
Install a monitoring agent via SSH in function
CloudWatch Lambda Insights, enabled by layer/extension, collecting system metrics and invocation performance
AWS Trusted Advisor by function
